articleText:
[Hacker News — swiftrocks.com]
I've always aimed to keep the content of this blog neutral, but the issue I'll cover today is genuinely pissing me off. I apologize in advance for the more aggressive tone that this post will have because I think it's necessary in this to get the point across.

If someone is assigned a task, be it to review a PR, work on a reasonably complex coding task, or even just asked a simple question, and all they do is prompt the agent "do X" and copy-paste the results back to you , with zero guidance or validation on behalf of the human (meaning it was 100% handled by the agent), and sometimes not even disclosing that this was the case , in my opinion this should be grounds for getting the dev in question punished in some capacity, and potentially even fired in more serious cases.

No, I'm not talking about the usual AI-assisted workflow which is commonplace nowadays where the human guides the agent, corrects it, reviews what comes out of it and opens PRs based on something that has been properly validated and cleaned up for other humans to review. I'm talking about the scenario where the human was nothing more than a meat proxy between you and whatever agent they used, making you feel that the person added no value and you should've just launched an agent yourself and skipped them entirely. They might have even potentially made things worse for you by doing so, and in more egregious cases even sometimes attempted to use this as a way to strip themselves of any responsibility regarding the code they write and merge (e.g. "This code broke master and took down production? It was opened and merged under my user? No, you see, it's not my problem because it was the AI who did this, not me! :)").

This shit is becoming increasingly prevalent in the software engineering industry and it's ruining software jobs. IMO this behavior should be punished because devs who do this are:

I always saw the software engineering field as being comprised of two groups of people: people who are devs because they are passionate about building software, and people who don't actually enjoy software but joined the field because it's a job that pays well. The latter being something that I find to be a perfectly fine thing to do as long as, you know, you actually do your job. Pre-AI, although sometimes I've found people in this group to not have been doing a particularly impressive job, they were still doing it nonetheless. So things were fine then.

But now that AI is widespread, I've been bumping into many folks who basically weaponized AI to make it seem like to their managers they are being extremely productive by opening hundreds of PRs with very complex descriptions and bold claims of having fixed major issues and/or greatly improved systems, when in reality a deeper look reveals that this "work" is actually just a bunch of unreviewed vibe-coded nonsense that not only doesn't fix or improves anything at all, but also actively harms whatever products they are "working" with and massively complicates the work of the devs who have to deal with the consequences of said garbage code and actually care about building good products and using AI responsibly.

This is getting so insane that I've even had cases where I would DM someone on Slack and notice right away that I'm talking to an AI. Not in the sense that they've set up an agent to handle their messages for them (wouldn't be surprised if people start doing this though), but that they are copying my question to an agent and pasting back the response (without disclosure, so making it seem that they wrote it themselves). WTF?

When chatting about this problem with colleagues, some of them suggested that the answer might be to throw AI back at the person (so if you get a barrage of unreviewed AI-generated review comments on your PR, throw another unreviewed AI-generated barrage of AI responses back at the person). But I feel that this just makes everything worse. It may get the PR itself out of your hands, but the code will suffer as a result and you'd still have to end up dealing with the consequences of that.

I don't understand why someone who doesn't like their job would try so hard to come up with ways to not do it that they would be fine with messing up their colleagues' work in order to achieve it. Nobody is forcing anyone to work in tech. If someone doesn't like it, they can just quit and do something they actually enjoy. It's what I would've done at least if I was in their situation.
reactions: [Hacker News] The linked post describes being a meat proxy as copypasting tickets into AI and pushing the output without reading. I don't copypaste tickets to AI, I decide on how each task is solved and LLMs only implement what I decided on. I read the code before making a PR. I review other's PR with my own eyes. I never copypaste LLM output to my coworkers in chat. What else is there to it?
[Hacker News] And how would they understand them if they didn't even read them?

[Hacker News] This is my problem with it, I can’t tell if people actually think the LLMs writing all their code is the future or they just want it to be the future because they’d prefer not to think and still get a dopamine hit from it.
[Hacker News] A compiler is deterministic, even if you don’t understand the assembly at least it will do exactly the same thing every time. I absolutely loath this comparison.

[Hacker News] I have worked for a few companies in my life and that just wasn't my experience in any of them. People tend to trust your judgment when you show that you know what you're talking about, and the use of agents to generate your output seems detrimental to that.

[Hacker News] What if I, as someone employing you, don't specifically need someone to look at the code? We may not be quite there yet, but what if automations using LLMs can do it faster than software engineers who look at the code can, and to an acceptable standard? > all while the same people acting like they’re productive. items.title: Being a meat proxy for AI should be grounds for getting people fired
